key_terms.meaning: For a stable linear system, the steady output to input A sin ωt is A|G(jω)| sin(ωt + ∠G(jω)); the function G(jω) is found by putting s = jω in G(s).
Numbers read off |G(jω)| and ∠G(jω): resonant peak Mr, resonant frequency ωr, bandwidth ωb, cut-off frequency, gain margin, phase margin.
Largest value of |G(jω)|; for a second-order system with 0 ≤ ζ < 0.707, Mr = 1/(2ζ√(1−ζ²)).
Frequency at which |G(jω)| is maximum: ωr = ωn√(1−2ζ²) rad/s, which exists only for ζ < 0.707.
Frequency where |G(jω)| falls to 1/√2 (−3 dB) of its value at ω = 0; ωb = ωn√(1−2ζ²+√(4ζ⁴−4ζ²+2)) rad/s for second order.
The −3 dB frequency of a low-pass magnitude curve; for a simple second-order system it is the same number as the bandwidth.
Two curves drawn against log₁₀ ω: 20 log₁₀|G(jω)| in dB, and ∠G(jω) in degrees.
Gain unit defined by dB = 20 log₁₀|G(jω)|; |G| = 10 gives 20 dB, |G| = 0.1 gives −20 dB.
A decade is a frequency change of ×10; an octave is a frequency change of ×2. Slopes on a Bode plot are quoted in dB/decade.
Break frequency 1/T where the straight-line approximation of a first-order factor (1 + jωT) changes slope; the true curve is 3 dB below the asymptote there.
The locus traced by the tip of the complex vector G(jω) in the complex plane while ω runs from 0 to ∞.
The closed path made of the whole jω axis plus a semicircle of infinite radius through the right half of the s-plane, used to apply the principle of the argument to 1 + G(s)H(s).
A point is encircled once when the closed locus makes one full turn around it; clockwise and anticlockwise turns are counted with opposite signs.
Z = P − N: Z is the number of closed-loop poles in the right half-plane, P the open-loop right-half-plane poles, and N the clockwise encirclements of −1 by the Nyquist plot. Stable needs Z = 0.
The frequency where ∠G(jω)H(jω) = −180°.
The frequency where |G(jω)H(jω)| = 1 (0 dB).
GM = −20 log₁₀|G(jωpc)H(jωpc)| dB; the extra gain in dB that can be added before the closed loop becomes unstable.
PM = 180° + ∠G(jωgc)H(jωgc); the extra phase lag in degrees that can be added at gain crossover before instability.
In the G(jω)H(jω) plane, the locus of open-loop points for which the closed-loop magnitude |T(jω)| = |G/(1+G)| equals a fixed value M.
The locus of open-loop points giving a fixed closed-loop phase N = ∠(G/(1+G)); M and N circles together turn an open-loop plot into a closed-loop plot.
A grid of open-loop gain (dB) against open-loop phase (degrees) carrying M and N contours, so the closed-loop response and bandwidth are read directly from the open-loop curve.

takeaways: A stable linear system fed a sine wave returns a sine wave of the same frequency, changed only in amplitude by |G(jω)| and in phase by ∠G(jω).
Frequency-domain numbers are not decoration: Mr and ωb of a second-order system fix overshoot and settling time, so a specification written in one domain can be met in the other.
The Bode plot is popular because logarithms turn the multiplication of factors in G(jω) into addition of straight-line segments that can be sketched by hand.
A polar plot shows magnitude and phase together as one curve, which is compact but loses the clear frequency scale that a Bode plot keeps.
The Nyquist criterion counts encirclements of −1 and settles closed-loop stability even when the open-loop transfer function itself is unstable.
Gain margin and phase margin are distances from the critical point −1, so they measure relative stability, not just yes-or-no stability.
M circles, N circles and the Nichols chart give the closed-loop frequency response straight from the open-loop curve without computing T(s).
Only a few universities go deep into Nichols chart reading; almost all syllabi insist on Bode sketching, polar sketching and the Nyquist criterion.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a clean sketch with the governing formula — for example a Bode sketch with margins computed from it, or a Nyquist plot with the count Z = P − N clearly tabulated.

bank.q: Define frequency response of a linear system. Show that a stable linear system driven by a sinusoidal input gives a sinusoidal output of the same frequency, and state how amplitude and phase change.
outline: Take G(s) with input A sin ωt written as the imaginary part of A e^{jωt}
Steady-state output is A|G(jω)| sin(ωt + ∠G(jω))
Transient terms decay because the system is stable
Define G(jω) by substituting s = jω and give magnitude and phase expressions
State that frequency response is measured by feeding sine waves and recording amplitude ratio and phase shift

bank.q: List and define the standard frequency-domain specifications of a second-order system and give the formula for each.
outline: Resonant peak Mr = 1/(2ζ√(1−ζ²)), valid for ζ < 0.707
Resonant frequency ωr = ωn√(1−2ζ²)
Bandwidth ωb formula and meaning of the −3 dB point
Cut-off frequency and its link to bandwidth
Gain margin and phase margin as further specifications
State clearly which specifications exist only for small ζ

bank.q: Give the rules for sketching the Bode plot of a transfer function written in time-constant form, and explain why straight-line approximations are possible.
outline: Convert G(s) to time-constant form and fix the low-frequency asymptote from the type number and gain K
Each pole or zero at 1/T adds a corner at ω = 1/T
Slopes: ±20 dB/decade per simple pole or zero, ±40 for repeated ones
Phase contribution of each factor: 0° to ±90° spread over one decade around the corner
Quadratic factor: slope change 40 dB/decade with peak near ωn for small ζ
Why it works: log of a product is a sum of logs, so segments add

bank.q: State the Nyquist stability criterion and explain the meaning of N, P and Z with a sign convention.
outline: Statement Z = P − N
P is the number of open-loop poles in the right half-plane
N is the number of clockwise encirclements of the point −1
Z is the number of closed-loop poles in the right half-plane
Stability requires Z = 0, so N = P
Note that a clockwise encirclement is positive and anticlockwise is negative

bank.q: Explain M circles and N circles, and describe how the Nichols chart is used to obtain the closed-loop frequency response from the open-loop frequency response.
outline: Closed-loop T(jω) = G/(1+G) with G the open-loop value
Derive or state the M-circle equation in the G-plane and sketch a family of M circles
Same for N circles giving constant closed-loop phase
Plot the open-loop G(jω) on the Nichol's grid of gain versus phase
Read intersections with M contours to get closed-loop magnitude versus frequency
Bandwidth is the frequency where the closed-loop magnitude falls to −3 dB

bank.q: Sketch the Bode plot of G(s)H(s) = K/[s(s+1)(s+2)] and find the value of K for a gain margin of 20 dB.
outline: Write in time-constant form and identify corner frequencies 1 rad/s and 2 rad/s
Low frequency slope −20 dB/decade, then −40, then −60 dB/decade
Find phase crossover frequency from ∠GH = −180°
Compute |GH| at that frequency and set −20 log₁₀|GH| = 20 dB
Solve for K and state the units and result clearly
Mention that the sketch must show the gain crossover point and margins

bank.q: A unity feedback second-order system has ωn = 5 rad/s and ζ = 0.2. Compute Mr, ωr and bandwidth, and hence estimate percentage overshoot and settling time. Comment on the correlation between the two domains.
outline: ωr = ωn√(1−2ζ²) ≈ 4.58 rad/s
Bandwidth from the standard second-order formula
Percentage overshoot = e^{−πζ/√(1−ζ²)} × 100 ≈ 52%
Settling time ts ≈ 4/(ζωn) = 4 s for 2% band
Conclusion: larger Mr and larger ωb mean larger overshoot and smaller rise time, so frequency specifications predict time behaviour

bank.q: Sketch the polar plot of G(s)H(s) = K/[s(1+Ts)] and explain its shape, starting point and end point, and how the plot changes with K.
outline: At ω → 0 the magnitude → ∞ and phase → −90°, so the plot starts at infinity along the negative imaginary axis
At ω → ∞ magnitude → 0 and phase → −180°
Intermediate points computed at ω = 1/T and ω = 1/√3T where the curve crosses the real axis
Curve is a semicircle-like locus approaching −180° asymptotically
Changing K scales the plot radially without changing its shape
State that for the type-1 case there is no real-axis crossing except the origin

bank.q: Using the Nyquist criterion, find the range of K for which the closed-loop system with G(s)H(s) = K/[s(s+1)(s+2)] is stable.
outline: Draw the Nyquist path: jω axis plus infinite right-half-plane semicircle
Sketch the open-loop locus for ω from 0+ to ∞, add its mirror image
Find the frequency where the locus crosses the negative real axis
Magnitude at that crossing is K/6, phase −180°
For no encirclement of −1 the crossing must lie to the right of −1, giving K < 6
Take the infinite semicircle into account: it maps to the origin since the system is type 1 with three poles
State the final range 0 < K < 6 and explain the reasoning

bank.q: Compare Bode plots, polar plots and Nyquist plots for frequency-response work. Which one would you choose for hand sketching, for stability testing of an unstable open loop, and for reading margins? Justify.
outline: Bode: separate gain and phase against log ω, factors add, margins read directly, frequency scale explicit
Polar: magnitude and phase shown together, compact, but frequency is lost and sketching is tedious
Nyquist: closed contour lets the criterion handle open-loop unstable plants through Z = P − N
Choose Bode for sketching and for margins
Choose Nyquist when P > 0 or when the contour must be closed
Note that all three carry the same information for a stable open loop

bank.q: A feedback system has a gain margin of 6 dB and a phase margin of 15°. Evaluate its relative stability and suggest, without designing a compensator, how the margins and Mr would change if the loop gain were reduced.
outline: Interpret GM = 6 dB as gain could be doubled before instability
PM = 15° is small, so the response is highly oscillatory with large Mr
Rule of thumb linking PM and ζ, hence overshoot and Mr
Reducing overall gain moves the magnitude curve down and ωgc to a lower frequency
Phase margin increases as ωgc moves left on a typical phase curve; Mr falls
Trade-off: lower gain also means larger steady-state error and larger rise time
Conclude with a judgement: the system is stable but poorly damped

bank.q: Derive the relation between Mr and ζ for a second-order system and discuss what happens to Mr, ωr and bandwidth as ζ goes from 0 to 1.
outline: Write |G(jω)| for the standard second-order closed-loop transfer function
Differentiate the denominator with respect to ω² and set to zero
Obtain ωr = ωn√(1−2ζ²) and Mr = 1/(2ζ√(1−ζ²))
Show that ωr and Mr exist only for ζ < 0.707, Mr → ∞ as ζ → 0
As ζ → 1, Mr → 1 and ωr → 0, bandwidth stays finite
Hence Mr is a damping indicator: large Mr means low damping and large overshoot

bank.q: Explain how the Nyquist criterion copes with a system whose open-loop transfer function has poles in the right half-plane, and show by an example how the number of encirclements is counted.
outline: Need to close the contour through the right half-plane, with small semicircles around imaginary-axis poles
P is counted from the open-loop poles with positive real part
N counted with the clockwise-positive convention on the full closed curve
Example: plant with one right-half-plane pole requires one clockwise encirclement of −1
Table of P, N, Z for the worked case and the stability conclusion
Explain that a Bode plot alone cannot decide stability when P > 0

bank.q: The open-loop transfer function of a unity feedback system is G(s) = 100/[s(s+2)(s+10)]. Find the gain and phase crossover frequencies, the gain margin and the phase margin, and state whether the closed loop is stable.
outline: Write in time-constant form and identify corners at 2 and 10 rad/s
Phase at ω gives ωpc from ∠G = −180°
Magnitude at ωpc gives GM in dB
Set |G| = 1 to get ωgc and compute PM = 180° + ∠G(jωgc)
Positive GM and PM mean stable
Comment on how small the PM is and what it says about damping

glossary.def: The condition reached after transients die out, when every signal in a stable linear system is a sine wave of the input frequency.
The complex ratio of output sine to input sine at each frequency, written G(jω).
How far a stable system is from the edge of instability, measured by gain and phase margins.
Whether the system is stable or unstable at all, without reference to how stable.
The maximum value of the closed-loop magnitude curve.
The frequency at which the magnitude curve reaches its peak.
The range of frequencies over which the magnitude stays within 1/√2 of its low-frequency value.
The upper frequency of the bandwidth, where the magnitude is −3 dB.
Twenty times the base-10 logarithm of a magnitude ratio.
A factor of ten in frequency.
A factor of two in frequency.
The frequency 1/T at which a first-order factor begins to change the Bode slope.
The straight line that a Bode segment approaches at very low or very high frequency.
A system with no poles or zeros in the right half of the s-plane, so its gain and phase are uniquely linked.
The path of G(jω) in the complex plane as frequency runs from zero to infinity.
The contour made of the jω axis and a large right-half-plane semicircle used in the Nyquist test.
A full turn of a closed locus about a point, counted with sign by direction.
The point −1 + j0 in the open-loop plane, whose encirclement decides closed-loop stability.
The frequency at which the open-loop magnitude equals one.
The frequency at which the open-loop phase equals minus 180 degrees.
The factor by which loop gain may rise before the closed loop becomes unstable, expressed in dB.
The phase lag that may be added at gain crossover before the closed loop becomes unstable.
A locus of constant closed-loop magnitude drawn in the open-loop plane.
A gain-versus-phase grid with M and N contours for reading closed-loop response from open-loop data.
A system that is stable for a middle range of gain but unstable for both very small and very large gain.
